# Madhura Sutta (MN 84 (PTS MN ii 83))

**ID:** MN 84 (PTS MN ii 83)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Madhura Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** At Madhurā
**PTS:** MN ii 83
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0202m.mul3.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Madhura Sutta* (MN 84) is a discourse set in Madhurā, towards the north-western limit of the Buddha's reach during his lifetime. It depicts a dialogue between King Avantiputta of Madhurā—identified in the commentary as the grandson of King Candappajjota of Avantī—and the Venerable Mahākaccāna [Dutt 1924; Nyanaponika et al. 2003]. The sutta is explicitly framed as occurring after the Buddha's final release (*parinibbāna*): when Avantiputta asks about the Master's whereabouts, Mahākaccāna explains that the Buddha has attained final *nibbāna* [Norman 1983; Nyanaponika et al. 2003; von Hinüber 1996]. Because it clearly postdates the Buddha's death, scholars frequently cite MN 84 alongside texts like MN 108 and MN 124 as clear canonical evidence of material composed or finalized after the First Council [Bodhi 2003; Norman 1983; von Hinüber 1996].

The central discussion focuses on the brahmanical claim to innate caste supremacy [Norman 1983; Obeyesekere 2002]. Paralleling the Buddha's critique in the *Assalāyana Sutta* (MN 93), Mahākaccāna dismantles these pretensions pragmatically, pointing out the social and ethical realities of wealth, moral retribution, and the monastic community [Norman 1983; Obeyesekere 2002]. Specifically, he demonstrates that if a person of any caste, including a Sūdra, goes forth as an ascetic (*samaṇa*), kings and society accord them equal honour and protection, dissolving prior caste designations [Dutt 1924; Obeyesekere 2002; Olivelle 1974].
